Brief Review

A Ronin requests to commit seppuku at a feudal lord's palace and tells the counselor of the clan's estate a story of how he came to be ready to take his own life.

Story

Set in 1630's Japan, an unemployed samurai (Hanshiro Tsugumo) enters the grounds of the Li clan's estate to ask if he can use their courtyard to commit seppuku. The counselor (Kageyu Saito) agrees to see Hanshiro to find out if he was serious or was trying to swindle the clan of money or services. Hanshiro explained to Kageyu that his after his former clan was disbanded he fell on hard times and wanted to have an honorable death. Kageyu asked if the knew the name Motome Chijiiwa because not a few weeks earlier another ronin showed up asking for the same and was from the same clan as Hanshiro and that Motome never had any intentions of committing seppuku. Three memebers (Hayato Yazaki, Umenosuke Kawabe, and Hikokuro Omodaka) found out this was a ruse when they discovered that his swords were in fact bamboo and not real. The three members forced Motome to commit seppuku using his own bamboo swords. After telling Hanshiro the story of Motome asked if he was still serious and Hanshiro persisted that he was serious about wanting to commit seppuku. Kegeyu agreed to let Hanshiro use their courtyard but required all top officials to be witnesses.

Hanshiro is sitting in the middle of the courtyard and asks who the second will be. The role of the second is to decapitate the samurai after their self inflicted disembowelment. Hanshiro requested to have a specific person to be the second and so Kageyu sent a messenger to fetch Hayato Yazaki because he was not present. As they waited, Hanshiro decided to tell everyone present his story that ultimately brought him there. He admitted that he actually did in fact know Motome Chijiiwa, but was more familiar with his father as they were close friends. Hanshiro was raising a daughter, Miho, who was a few years younger than Motome. The shogun had disbanded Hanshiro's clan and the retainer was ordered to commit seppuku and Hanshiro was going to follow but instead Motome's father committed seppuku and instructed Hanshiro to continue raising Motome.

I'm going to leave it here because it's hard to talk about the story without spoiling huge parts of the movie.

What Was Good

I could not find anything bad with this movie. The story was great as it brought into question just what does honor among samurai truly mean. That saving appearances are sometimes more important to a clan's image than doing the right thing. The pacing of the movie was fantastic. They did an excellent job with moving the story between present time and past. It was clear as Hanshiro was telling his story that he was flashing back. He had a different tone in his voice between then and now and you knew as he was speaking, it was to continue with the telling of his story. Even the subtitles were well translated and properly timed. There really wasn't much bad with this movie.

What Was Bad

While there was much bad, I do need to mention some things that could have been better. There isn't much of a soundtrack. That's not to say there isn't any music, but its very sparse. Also, there's one sound that you hear often that sounds like a twig snapping, but really loud. It was Kageyu's fan, he would snap it closed. Sometimes that sound would be a bit too loud.

Also, there isn't much fighting. This is a story driven movie, only reserving the combat for the end.

Final Thoughts

I had always heard about this movie was I never got around to watching it. I'm kicking myself for not having watched it sooner. I could not look away the entire time. The 2 hour run time seemed to have flew by as I was wanting to see how everything would play out. I was not disappointed at all.

If you want a combat heavy samurai movie, this isn't for you. But, if you are looking for a good drama samurai time period movie, this is one of the best and you won't be disappointed.
